notes: Woodfolk forester at Fernhold; main quest 6. Restraint as a virtue and a vice: the notched bow-stave and the silence that lets wrongs stand.

greetings.text: Rosen's teaching. Listen to her; I never have, and look at me.
Keep low. This is the Briar, and it is listening.
You've seen it. Don't say anything yet.
So I was not wrong. I will have to live with that. So will you.
You named me keeper of a circle I have oiled for thirty years and never stood in the middle of. I have stood in the middle of it now. Once.
Empty centre. The Wold has not decided what it thinks. Neither have I, and I am usually faster than the Wold.
The Hart is down. Thirty years I walked round that circle at a distance out of manners. Come in; there is meat and you will eat it.
Nineteen grey patches. It was fourteen at midwinter. You have seen it now, so I need not describe it, which I am glad of.
You may stand at the rail. There is a rail for a reason and today you are the reason.

greet.speaker: Alder Wyke
greet.text: Wyke. Fernhold's forester. We have no law here, only custom and bows, and you will find the custom is mostly common sense and the bows are mostly mine.

choices.text: What are you counting?
The hart. What's happened to it?
Tell me about the Briar.
Why are you notching your bow-stave?
What is the Standing Moot's custom?
What is the Hart of Thorns?
The Woodfolk have no law at all?
I'll walk on.

count_the_grey.speaker: Alder Wyke
count_the_grey.text: Grey patches. There. A hand's width of the Briar gone the colour of old ash, thorns and leaf and all, and nothing wrong with it you could put a knife to. Eighteen yesterday. — Nineteen. — The Oroth grew this wall to keep the Hush in the south, and the wall is going grey from the inside, a hand's width at a time, and I count it because counting is the only thing I know how to do about it. See the slots in the mud? A hart, walking. Big. Remember them.

hart_ask.speaker: Alder Wyke
hart_ask.text: That's the hart whose slots you read. It's gone grey. Not old: grey, the way the Briar goes. It came out of the wood and it's going south, and it isn't running from anything, which is the worst thing I have seen a hart do. — Follow it. Find where it goes. I know where it goes, and I want to be wrong. Take the road; it will. Rosen's pony knows it.

the_briar.speaker: Alder Wyke
the_briar.text: A wall of living thorn along the whole eastern rim, vines thick as your arm, grown on purpose by people who wrote no purpose down. — I walk it every morning and count the grey patches: where the thorn has gone brittle and colourless and the birds go round. Fourteen at midwinter. Nineteen now. — The Oroth books say it was raised to keep something out. The Sedgish songs say it was raised to keep the Dwindling in, in the south, where it started. I have walked that wall for thirty years and I will tell you which way the dead thorn falls, which is inward, and you may make of that what a forester makes of it.

the_notches.speaker: Alder Wyke
the_notches.text: One for every animal I chose not to shoot. — It is nearly through in one place and I will have to start a second stave, which I have been putting off for two years like a coward. — Restraint is our virtue. You will hear us say so. What we say less is the other side of it: a people who are very good at not acting are also very good at watching a thing go wrong for eleven years and saying nothing, out of manners. I have a notch for every hare. I have no mark at all for the years I watched the grey patches spread and told nobody outside this wood.

the_moot.speaker: Alder Wyke
the_moot.text: The stones hum if you stand in the middle. Custom says the circle will answer one question of whoever stands at the centre at dusk and is still standing at dark. — Nobody has ever managed it, because the Hart of Thorns keeps that circle and has kept it since before we had a word for keeping. We oil the stones. We do not stand in them. That is thirty years of my life summarised for a stranger in nine words and it does not sound like very much when it is said aloud.

the_hart.speaker: Alder Wyke
the_hart.text: Antlered plate, a spear, and a charge that will put you through a stone. — He is not a villain. I want that said before you go up there with a weapon in your hand. He is a keeper who has forgotten what he is keeping the circle from, and that is a thing that happens to keepers, and it will happen to me if I am lucky enough to last. — Use the stones. He charges straight and he cannot help it. And when the Briar grows across the ring in the second half of it, count the ground you have left, because it will be half what you think.

no_law.speaker: Alder Wyke
no_law.text: None. No court, no fine, no cell. If you take more than you need out of this wood, the first time somebody tells you. The second time nobody tells you anything, and you will find the lodges shut and the paths harder than you remember, and that goes on until you leave or learn. — It works. I will not pretend it is kind. A man at the charcoal camp beat his wife for six years and what we did about it was stop selling him rope, and she left in the end on her own feet and no thanks to any of us and I think about it most weeks.

bye.speaker: Alder Wyke
bye.text: Go quietly. Not for the deer. There are things in the deep of this wood that only wake for a loud walker, and you would not be the first to teach them the shape of a person.

notes: Quiet Hands door-keeper; gives The Unsaid Ledger. Never says her own name or the player's, and calls everyone by the last thing they touched.

greetings.text: Thimble. Sit on the step. There is a step for people who have carried something.
...Door. The door is behind you and it is the last thing you touched and it is the last thing you will touch down here.
Railing. You put it back. That is not nothing and it is not enough, and both of those are going in the book.
Lamp-post. You are standing in the light again. We have discussed the light.
Loud one. You cannot Hush at that volume; it is like asking a bonfire to be a candle. We shall have to find you other work.

greet.speaker: Half-Ell
greet.text: Handrail. — That is you, now, until you touch something else. I do not use names down here and neither will you, and you will find out why on your own, which is the only way anybody believes it.

choices.text: Why won't you use names?
What is the door that opens for names?
Teach me Hush.
What is the Unsaid Ledger?
Give me work.
I have the day-book.
Four marks and forty. Why did the fisher pay?
The chit is in Quill's own hand.
What is behind the back of the bell hall?
There is a second door in the bell's side.
Then let us go and get the Ledger.
Thirty-one marks in the pound.
I'm going up.

the_daybook.speaker: Half-Ell
the_daybook.text: Day-book. — That is you now and it will be you for the rest of the evening. Hold it up; I am not going to touch it until it is decided. — Four marks for a Merrowby carter and forty for a Gullhithe fisher for the same barrow in the same street in the same week, with a note in the margin about who each of them knows. That is one week. There are four thousand seven hundred of them upstairs in a book with brass corners. — It is yours to place. That is not a test and there is no answer I want, and if you believe that you are the first person down here who ever has.

choices.text: It goes to the Hands. Let it be read.
I'm putting it back on Quill's desk.
I am taking it to Quill and telling him who wanted it.
Give me the night with it.

daybook_to_hands.speaker: Half-Ell
daybook_to_hands.text: Then it goes in the press with the other four thousand seven hundred, and you go on the step, and there is a thimble on the step which is worth more down here than the marks in your purse. — Doors open for a thimble. Not because it is a key; because the four people who would stop you have all seen one and know what it cost. — Fingers, then. Lowest rank we have, and the only one I have ever been glad to hand out.

daybook_returned.speaker: Half-Ell
daybook_returned.text: Railing. — Put it back where the ring of the lamp-base is on the desk, or he will know within the hour, and he is a man who writes down what he knows. — I am not angry and I am going to be honest about why, which is that half the Hands have done exactly that once and the ones who did not are the ones I watch. You are not in. You are also not out, and you will find that is the worse of the two.

daybook_to_quill.speaker: Half-Ell
daybook_to_quill.text: ...Door. — The door is behind you. It is the last thing you touched and it will be the last thing you touch down here, and you may go out through it now while everybody in this hall is still being extremely polite. — Fifty marks. He gave you fifty marks for a week of his own prices and the name of a woman he cannot find. You could have had the whole book.

two_fines_offer.speaker: Half-Ell
two_fines_offer.text: Because he was buying something. — Forty marks is a boat. A man who is fined a boat and pays it without going to the Guild hall to shout is a man who was told what the fine was for, and it was not for a barrow. Nobody reported anything; that is the whole shape of it. A theft nobody reports did not happen, and a fine nobody argues with is a receipt. — I have had that page for two years. It never once occurred to me to go to Gullhithe and ask the man whose name is on it, and I would like somebody to go and ask him, and I would like to be irritated about not having thought of it.

choices.text: I'll go and ask him.
Why has nobody asked him?
Not tonight.

two_fines_why.speaker: Half-Ell
two_fines_why.text: Because we read the book and not the people in it. — Three hundred years of copying the Guild's arithmetic and we have got very good at arithmetic. There is a column in the Ledger headed regard and we can tell you to the mark what a name is worth in this city, and not one of us could tell you what the fisher's boat is called. — Go and ask him. Say the figure to him; he says it every morning himself, which somebody in the Row thinks is Vale nonsense and which is the only reason his fine is still a live thing and not a page.

choices.text: Then I'll go.
Later.

two_fines_accept.speaker: Half-Ell
two_fines_accept.text: Gullhithe, the racks, and a man who will be on the water until noon. Wait on the shingle; the lake does not. — And if he sends you somewhere, go there in daylight. Whatever was landed with a seal already on it was landed by people who buy their seals, and people who buy seals do not mind what they pay for quiet.

whose_hand.speaker: Half-Ell
whose_hand.text: Lay it beside the page. — There. The same hand that wrote *unchartered; sells direct* in a margin wrote *weighed, taxed and sealed* on a chit for a cargo that never came through the Row. — He is not a thief. I want that understood, because down here it is a compliment and I do not hand them out. He is a man who has been totalling the price of the law for twenty years and has started paying it himself, and what we do with him is the only decision in this business that has ever kept me up.

choices.text: Keep it. A steward who can be shown his own hand is a door.
The paid watch can have it. Let the law price its own steward.
Jory Wick can have it. It is worth forty marks to exactly one man.
Give me a day.

hand_settled.speaker: Half-Ell
hand_settled.text: Then that is where it goes, and it is in the book as yours, because the Hands write down who decided a thing even when they will not write down a name. — Palm. Second of five, and the first rank that is a hand and not a finger. It is not for the chit. It is for going to Gullhithe.

the_wall_offer.speaker: Half-Ell
the_wall_offer.text: That is the question I have been carrying round the outside of this hall for twenty years. — The bell is one piece. Builder-work, fallen, and we live in it, and you can walk the whole way round the inside. You cannot walk the whole way round the outside, because at the back of it the stone is new and coursed and somebody cut it, and it is not our coursing. — Guild work, and the Guild writes everything down, and everything the Guild writes down gets copied on Lantern Row by a woman who copies everything and charges for the paper.

choices.text: I'll get the entry off the binder.
Not yet.

the_wall_accept.speaker: Half-Ell
the_wall_accept.text: Nine hundred and ninety-eight, or thereabouts; ask for the strongroom and she will know the number better than I do. — And come back down the way you went up. If the thing behind that wall is what I have stopped myself believing for twenty years, I do not want the first person who knows to be a clerk.

whose_name.speaker: Half-Ell
whose_name.text: There is, and it is smaller, and it has no hinges, and the Guild has coursed its own back wall straight across it without ever once seeing it, because the Guild looks for doors. — It opens for names. I am not going to say one to it. That is not superstition, and I will say the reason out loud once and then not again: I have not heard my whole name said in twenty years, and I do not know any more whether that door would find anything to open for, and I would rather not learn it standing in a crawl at four in the morning.

choices.text: I'll say mine. It opens for the known.
Say Quill's. If the Guild has been through, his will open it.
No names. We cut the Guild's coursing out and go in through their wall.
Let me sit with that.

name_settled.speaker: Half-Ell
name_settled.text: Then the way in is open and nobody is going in tonight. — I want one night in this hall knowing what is on the other side of the wall I have leaned on for twenty years. You may think that is sentiment. It is that I have been told my whole life that being unsaid is a price you pay for a hall nobody can find, and it turns out the Guild found it in 998, built against it, and wrote down the measurements. — Quiet Hand. Middle rank. The only one where anybody is any use.

last_heist_offer.speaker: Half-Ell
last_heist_offer.text: Then let us. — Ninety-one years, eleven hands, brass corners, and a fourth column headed regard that is the whole reason it has never been nailed to a board. Two of the Guild's bravos stand in that room and have done for nine years and they are within their charter, which is worth knowing: they will offer you a duel and a Tallyman in a frame on the wall is the witness. — Take it. Read it. Then tell me who reads it after you, and be aware while you are deciding that I have argued both sides of that in this hall for twenty years and lost both times.

choices.text: In through the bell's side, then.
Why me?
Not yet.

last_heist_why.speaker: Half-Ell
last_heist_why.text: Arithmetic, and I have done it twice to be sure. — A book that is meant to be loud one day has to be carried out by somebody who can be heard. I am forty and nobody has said my whole name in twenty years and that was the fee and I paid it and I would pay it again, and it means that if I walk up on to the charter-board with the Ledger in my hands, a woman nobody can name nails up a book nobody will believe. — You are getting known. That is a tool and it is the only one in this hall I do not have.

choices.text: Then I'll carry it.
Let me think about it.

last_heist_accept.speaker: Half-Ell
last_heist_accept.text: Fourth step, then the crawl, then the Guild's footings, and there is no lamp in the bracket because they took the lamp away in 1012 and never put one back, which tells you how often anybody goes in. — Read it in the room if your nerve is good and on the step if it is not. Everybody says the room and everybody reads it on the step.

who_reads_it.speaker: Half-Ell
who_reads_it.text: Say it again. — Thirty-one marks in the pound. That is what being thought well of is worth in this city, averaged over ninety-one years, in the Guild's own arithmetic, in a book the Guild locked in a room with two duelists in it. — Everybody from the Vale to the Choir has been arranging their whole life around that number and not one of them has seen it. I have sat on this step for a week and I have not decided, and I am not going to pretend I am letting you decide as a kindness.

choices.text: It goes on the charter-board. Let the city read it.
The Hands keep it. The reading you have not done is the power.
The Guild buys it back. They will pay more than you can.
It burns. Nobody should be able to look that up.
One more night.

ledger_settled.speaker: Half-Ell
ledger_settled.text: Then it is decided, and the crawl gets bricked up tonight with the Guild's own limestone, which I have been looking forward to for a week. — Glove. Left-handed, worn through at the finger-ends on purpose so the fingers can feel a ward through it. We give one and keep the other and nobody will tell you where the other one is. — The Unsaid. Top of five. It is not a promotion, it is a description, and you will find out which in about a year.

ledger_sold.speaker: Half-Ell
ledger_sold.text: ...Six hundred marks. — Say nothing else. I am going to stand here while you count it, because I want to be able to say afterwards that I watched. — The crawl gets bricked up tonight either way. Mind the fourth step on your way out; it is a bad step and we have all agreed to keep it, and it is the last thing in this hall that will do you a kindness.

the_names.speaker: Half-Ell
the_names.text: Because every soul above this ceiling believes that being spoken of keeps you warm, and they are right, and warm things are easy to find. — We do the other thing. A Hand who is not named is not looked for, and a Hand who is not looked for can stand in a counting-house at noon. It costs. I have not heard my whole name said aloud in twenty years and there are mornings I have to write it down to be sure of it. That is the fee. I paid it. Nobody made me and nobody thanked me.

the_door.speaker: Half-Ell
the_door.text: Builder-work. No hinges, and it opens for names — say one at it and it considers. Yours works if you are known. If you are not, say the name of somebody who has wronged you; it finds that funny, and I have never once been able to explain why, and I have watched it happen four hundred times. — We built the hall behind it inside a fallen bell, which the guilds have never found, because the guilds look for doors.

the_hush.speaker: Half-Ell
the_hush.text: It is not magic, whatever the Circle sells. — You stand where nobody is looking, and you let the not-looking do the work. That is the first Hush and it is nine-tenths of all of it. People do not see what they have no reason to see; a man carrying a crate past a clerk is a crate. The rest is knowing which part of a room has no reason in it. — Come at the hour before the watch changes and I will show you the counting-house from the outside and you will see the place in the wall where nobody's eye goes. Then it is yours and I cannot take it back off you.

the_ledger.speaker: Half-Ell
the_ledger.text: Every price the law has ever taken in this city, in one book, kept by us, added to since the Charter. — Not bribes. Prices. A fine of four marks for a Merrowby carter and forty for a Gullhithe fisher, same barrow, same street, same week, with a note in the margin about who each of them knows. The Tallymen do not hide it; they write it down, because a thing written down in a ledger stops looking like a decision. — We have been copying it for three hundred years and we have never published it, and the argument about whether to is the only argument the Hands have ever had that lasted longer than a night.

the_job.speaker: Half-Ell
the_job.text: Lantern Row. Steward Quill's day-book: one week of prices, fines and favours, in a small tidy hand, on a desk he does not lock because locking it would suggest something. — Take it without being seen. Not without being suspected; suspected is fine, suspected is most of my working life. Seen is what we mind. — And read it before you bring it down. The Hands will not object; a thing read by one more person is louder, and that book is meant to be loud one day.

bye.speaker: Half-Ell
bye.text: Mind the fourth step. It is not trapped. It is simply a bad step and we have all decided to keep it, because a bad step is worth two guards.

notes: Lamp keeper at Gullhithe; holds the lost name of Mullbourne in The Last Name side quest.

greetings.text: There's the braziers, there's you. I'm Tamsin. I keep the Lamp, and I'm no Sayer, so don't call me one. Say it at the near one. Go on.
Off the fells, and you've come down to the water to learn to shout at braziers. Well, the Mere won't mind. I'm Tamsin. Say it at the near one.
Woodfolk, and a long way from the trees, you. No shade on a headland. I'm Tamsin. Say it at the near one; it won't bite.
Ash on your boots, all the way up here. You'll find fire easier than most, then. I'm Tamsin. Say it at the near one.
Reedborn. You'll know water, then, and you'll know it doesn't burn. These do. I'm Tamsin. Say it at the near one.
Jory's on the shingle with his pockets full. Tell him to start. Ward first.
Drakes, off the wreck. Say the cold at them, under your breath. It doesn't like to be shouted.
Muffled oars. That's not fishermen. Keep the stair between you, and don't let them near my stone.
Is it quiet? It's quiet. Come up, then.
Morning. Put your ear to it. Go on, it's only brass.
The bell came back without its note. I held it up to the stone and it said nothing at all. I've never heard brass sulk.
They say the old Warden's saying three names again of a morning. Over in Merrowby. Forty mile off. And I'm the one who said it out loud first, on my own slipway, after fifty years of not.
I said it. I've said it now. It's out and it can go where it likes.
You're the one off the song. We got the song a month back off a Tollmere boat with two extra verses and a different tune, which is how everything gets here.
Come up. Mind the rail, it's wet, it's always wet. She's just lit and she's at her best in the first hour.

greet.speaker: Tamsin Wick
greet.text: Eels on the racks, light in the tower, and if you've come for either you're forty minutes early or two hours late, which is Gullhithe all over.

choices.text: How do I say it at the far one?
It's quiet on the shore. They had this in the boat.
What does the bell hear?
Tell me about the Lamp.
You say good evening to a stone.
Your family came off soft ground, inland.
What do the boats bring in?
The Lamp is dimmer, and you know it.
Four flakes are gone off the north face.
Right, I'll leave you to the eels.

braziers_help.speaker: Tamsin Wick
braziers_help.text: Look at it, not near it. Hold it in your eye and say it, and it goes where you're looking, like gossip. The pool's the thing that empties: every saying takes a cup out of it and your breathing puts it back, so don't stand there saying it at the sea. — And if it's far, it's far. It'll get there. Fire's patient. It's the only patient thing about it.

report_done.speaker: Tamsin Wick
report_done.text: A listening-bell. The Circle makes those to hear what a stone's saying to itself, and they'd hang a Sayer for selling one, which is why they were rowing it about in the dark. — You kept them off my stone. You didn't get in reach once. Well. Once. — Take Kettle. She pulled the eel-cart to Tollmere till the Tallymen priced the barrow off the Row, and she's been eating my hay ever since with nothing to pull. Sleep here. In the morning I want you to listen to that bell.

bell_help.speaker: Tamsin Wick
bell_help.text: My stone, when it's close. It hums a bit, the way a kettle does before it thinks about it. — But that's not what it's hearing this morning. Hold it up. It's got a note in it that isn't mine, a low one, and it's louder when you point it south. The Circle would charge you to hear that, and they'd be wrong about what it was.

the_lamp.speaker: Tamsin Wick
the_lamp.text: Builder-work in a human tower. The light's a sul-stone, about the size of a loaf, and it's been going since before there was a Gullhithe to shine at. I don't fuel it. I uncover it at dusk and cover it at dawn and turn the mirror by hand all night, and that's the whole trade, and it's thirty years of my life and I'd not swap it. — It's dimmer than it was. I'll say that to you and not to a Sayer, because a Sayer would want to come and measure it and I've seen what their measuring does to a thing that was working.

the_stone.speaker: Tamsin Wick
the_stone.text: Good evening when I uncover it, good morning when I cover it. Thirty years. — And it brightens for the good evening. Not for the good morning. Every night, a little lift, like a dog hearing the door. I've tested it and I've kept quiet at it and it doesn't lift, and I've said it in other words and it doesn't lift, and I've had my sister say it and it lifts for her too, so it's not me. — I don't know what that means and I've stopped needing to. Something in there likes being spoken to at the start of its work. There's worse things to be.

the_knife.speaker: Tamsin Wick
the_knife.text: ...My mother's mother. Come off the soft ground when the mill there failed, which is what they always said, the mill that never worked. Married a Gullhithe man and never went back and never talked of it. — There's a knife. Eel-knife, worn thin as a leaf, and the name's cut into the handle. I've had it in my hand every working day of my life. — And nobody has ever asked me. Fifty-eight years and not one soul has asked what's on the handle, and I never said it, because who says a thing nobody's asked? — Mullbourne. That's it. Mullbourne. Nine households and a well that tasted of iron. — Take it to the old man. Go on, before I want it back.

the_talk.speaker: Tamsin Wick
the_talk.text: Prices, weather, and whatever Tollmere's arguing about, three days stale. — And this, which you'll not get on the quay: the eels are running short and early, and the buoy bells out on the Mere have been ringing on still nights. Still nights. No swell. Four of us have heard it and we've agreed not to make anything of it, and I'm making something of it now, to you, because you've a sword and a look about you and you'll be gone by Tollday.

two_logbooks.speaker: Tamsin Wick
two_logbooks.text: ...Which of them told you. — Jory counted the turns. Of course he did; he has never counted them in his life and he counted them that morning and then came up my stair to tell me, which is the Wick family all over. — Yes. It is dimmer. It has been dimmer for two years and it is dimmer this month than last, and I keep two books: the Guild's, which goes down to Lantern Row every quarter, and mine, which does not, and neither of them says so, and I have been the keeper for thirty years and I know exactly what that sentence makes me.

choices.text: Why not write it in the Guild's book?
Let me find out what is wrong with it.
That is your business.

the_guilds_book.speaker: Tamsin Wick
the_guilds_book.text: Because a keeper who reports a dimming lamp is a keeper replaced by a guild one on a guild wage. — That is not fear for my post. I am sixty-one and I have a cottage and a niece who feeds me eels. It is that a guild keeper will be on that stair four nights a week and paid for four, and the Lamp wants somebody on it seven, and the difference between four and seven is a boat a winter, and I can name the winters. — I am not asking you to keep it quiet. I am telling you what I have been weighing at three in the morning for two years, and I would like somebody else to hold one end of it.

choices.text: Then let me find out what is wrong with it.
I will think about it.

the_lamp_accept.speaker: Tamsin Wick
the_lamp_accept.text: Ask on the shore first and not on the stair. Jory for the count and Elsie for the morning, and be gentle with Elsie; she was on the slipway and she has not been up to the light since and she will tell you it is because of the stairs. — Then go up the north cliff. I have been up there twice with a lamp and found nothing and come down, and both times I went in daylight, and I have worked out lately that this was a decision.

the_sliver.speaker: Tamsin Wick
the_sliver.text: Four flakes off the north face where nobody looks from. — Thirty years and I never once put a hand round the back of my own stone. — Right. Both books are open and I am going to do whatever you say, and I want to say before you answer that the dimming is not four flakes. It was going out before anybody chipped it. The chipping is a thief and I can write a thief in a book. The other thing I cannot write in a book at all, and there is one morning in thirty years when it got brighter, and it was a child saying good evening to it at the wrong end of the day.

choices.text: Write it in the Guild's book. A lit lake is worth a post.
Write nothing. Set the sliver back and keep your stair.
Let Elsie back up at dusk. It is the only thing that ever made it brighter.
Give me the night on it.

the_lamp_settled.speaker: Tamsin Wick
the_lamp_settled.text: Then that is what the book says, and the light goes round tonight the way it has gone round for thirty years, and every boat on that water counts it without knowing they are counting. — Take this. Wisp-glim, off the racks; Lettie has a jar of them and thinks they are pretty. It lights nothing and it is bright regardless, and I have never been able to decide whether that is a comfort.

the_lamp_elsie.speaker: Tamsin Wick
the_lamp_elsie.text: ...She is eight. — She came up every dusk she was allowed for two years and said good evening to it and I let her because it kept her off the shingle, and on Merrowday I covered it in the morning and it brightened, and she saw, and she has not been up since. — You are asking me to tell a frightened child that the thing she is frightened of got brighter because she was there. — I am going to do it. I am going to do it tonight, and I would like you on the stair behind me when I do, and then I am going to write that in my own book and not in the Guild's, because there is no column for it and because it is the first thing in thirty years I have wanted to write down.

bye.speaker: Tamsin Wick
bye.text: Go on. And if you're on the water after dark, watch for the sweep and count it: eleven seconds. If it's not eleven, come and tell me and I'll not thank you for it.

notes: Tallymen steward of Lantern Row. The mark he is lifted from in The Unsaid Ledger; not a villain, and his defence of the charter-board is the faction's best argument.

greetings.text: Four pins, a Guild mason and a clan elder, and they did not speak and did not need to. I posted the cost of the pins. It was the smallest figure on the board and the only one anybody read.

CHARTER STONE, BROKEN. Road toll, clans: see below. It is the largest figure I have ever posted, and the widows' line is the longest on the board. Every figure on it is true. I did not say I liked it.
Somebody from the Guild and somebody from Kharrow walk up to look at the Charter Stone every morning, from opposite ends of the road, at the same hour. I have posted the hour.
The man who handed it back with the name of who wanted it. The Guild has noted it. I have noted that the Guild noted it.
Good day. — You will forgive me; I am counting something and I find I am counting it twice today.
A celebrated person. Celebrated persons pay the posted price, which is the entire point of posting it.
The watch is at the end of the row and the watch is paid by the hour and I have written down the hour.

q_the_charter_pins_offer.speaker: Orrin Quill
q_the_charter_pins_offer.text: Four this month, one a night, and two left, and I have priced what it costs if the last two go. It is on a sheet in my desk. I will not show you; it has widows on it. — The Charter of 712. North of the Narrows, no toll; south of them, no blood-price. Both sides broke it and both sides mended it and both still go out to that stone to swear, which is the most honest thing either of them does. — Go and sit a night by it. And then look at the Counting Tower. Its clerk has stopped sending me figures, and a clerk who stops sending figures has either died or seen something.

choices.text: I'll sit a night at the stone.
Not now.

q_the_charter_pins_accept.speaker: Orrin Quill
q_the_charter_pins_accept.text: I will note your time from now. Not to charge you. To know what it cost.

q_the_charter_pins_decide_repin_it.speaker: Orrin Quill
q_the_charter_pins_decide_repin_it.text: Four pins, driven by a Guild mason and watched by a clan elder, which will be the first thing they have watched together since 942. I will post the cost. It will be small.

q_the_charter_pins_decide_let_it_break.speaker: Orrin Quill
q_the_charter_pins_decide_let_it_break.text: Then the board will carry a new line, and it will be the largest figure I have ever posted, and every figure on it will be true. — Here. The Guild pays finders. I did not say it paid well.

q_the_charter_pins_decide_two_pins.speaker: Orrin Quill
q_the_charter_pins_decide_two_pins.text: Two pins. — A charter held by two pins is a charter everybody is watching. That may be the best kind. I shall post it: CHARTER STONE, HELD, TWO PINS. Let the city do the arithmetic.

q_the_charter_pins_decide.speaker: Orrin Quill
q_the_charter_pins_decide.text: Owed back. — Something is keeping the city's accounts in the Builders' figures, at our own window, against a column we do not have. — I believe in the board because it does not pretend to be free. If the Charter goes, the board will say what the road costs in marks and blood, in public. I would post it. I would not like it. Say.

choices.text: Pin it again.
Let it break.
Leave it on two.
Let me think on it.

q_the_same_hand_the_city_end.speaker: Orrin Quill
q_the_same_hand_the_city_end.text: Give me the page. — Four minutes. — Eleven of them are on the rent-rolls, alive, paying, at the same addresses they took on arrival, which I find admirable. Eight are on the harbour roll, dead, in the city, of the usual things. Not one of the nineteen is on a Vale roll of anything, and I have the Rest's copy of the Roll in my desk because I price the Rest's parchment. — Every one of them went out along the Stride and was never said again in the place they came from. I have written you the figure. I will not charge you for it. It is not the kind of figure I charge for.

greet.speaker: Orrin Quill
greet.text: Quill, steward of Lantern Row. Prices are on the board, the board is posted at first light, and I do not adjust it for charm.

choices.text: Explain the charter-board.
You price the law differently for different people.
You're totalling our conversation.
What do the Tallymen want?
Who on this row works under charter?
Something is drawing the Charter Stone's pins.
A Sayer was drawing them. The tower is counting what's owed back.
Are these nineteen in the city?
Good day.

the_board.speaker: Orrin Quill
the_board.text: Every price the city charges, in public, at first light, in a hand large enough to read from the bridge. Fines, tolls, wharfage, the cost of a watchman for a night. — People call it cold. It is the most honest object in Tollmere and I will defend it to anyone who has lived somewhere without one. In a village the price of a thing is what the miller feels about you. Here it is on a board, and a Gullhithe fisher who cannot read can have it read to him by a stranger and know he has not been singled out. That is not a small thing. That is the only protection a poor man has ever had in this city.

the_prices.speaker: Orrin Quill
the_prices.text: ...We do. It is on the board, so I will not pretend otherwise; the pretending is what I would find shameful. — Four marks for a Merrowby carter, forty for a Gullhithe fisher, the same barrow in the same street. The reasoning written down is that the fisher's trade is unlicensed and the carter's is chartered. The reasoning is real and it is also a wall built where a wall was wanted. — I have raised it twice at the Guild. I was heard, courteously, both times, and the figure did not move, and I went back to my desk and wrote the figure up in a large clear hand at first light, because the alternative was not writing it up. I am not asking you to think well of that. I have not managed it myself.

the_book.speaker: Orrin Quill
the_book.text: I am. Greeting, four minutes, two questions of substance. I can show you the figure if you like; most people ask to see it and then wish they had not. — It is not avarice. It is that I was a clerk's son in Gullhithe and I watched my father be charged whatever a man felt like that morning for eleven years, and I decided that I would count everything and write it down where it could be seen. It has made me the least liked man on this row. My father could not have told you what anything cost. I can tell you what a conversation costs. One of us was cheated daily and it was not me.

the_guild.speaker: Orrin Quill
the_guild.text: Property, trade, prices, and a watch that is paid and therefore predictable, which is more than the Wardens' virtue will ever be. — We are not loved. We are the reason a woman in Isseva can send eels to Kharrow Hold and be paid a price she agreed to before the boat left. Every account of the Dwindling in that spire up there says the world holds together by being spoken of. Fine. A contract is a thing spoken of, in writing, by two people who do not trust each other, and it holds. Let the Circle put that in a lecture.

the_charters.speaker: Orrin Quill
the_charters.text: Fourteen trades. The list is posted under the fines, where nobody reads it, which I have raised at the Guild and been heard about courteously. — Two coopers. A ropewalk. Three chandlers, which is one chandler too many; the third will be gone by winter and I have written the date down. And at the canal end, Lathe, who makes the watch's crossbows and cuts the numbers into the stocks. — I will say a thing about her I would not say about the others. In nine years she has never once asked me to shave a figure for her, and she is the only trade on this row of whom that is true. I include myself in that count. I asked, once, about a lamp.

bye.speaker: Orrin Quill
bye.text: Good day. The board is reposted at first light; anything you were told before then was yesterday's.

notes: The last Fennick, in pilgrim grey at Pilgrim's Ash. Endpoint of Seventeen Bells and the escort in Vigil. Cheerful, unhurried, not to be talked out of it.

greetings.text: You carried it all this way and it never rang once. Well. It may ring on the other side. I shall listen for it.
They rang my bell in the chapter-house, out of custom, in the wrong month. I am told it woke everyone. I am delighted.
You again. Sit on the stone; the tents are full of people being solemn at each other.
Merrowby on you. The chalk dust sits in a seam on the shoulder and nowhere else. Forty years I brushed that off a doorstep.
You have kind hands. That is not a compliment, it is a diagnosis; I have been mending grey for six months and I can tell.

greet.speaker: Aud Fennick
greet.text: Aud Fennick, late of Merrowby, presently of a tent. Mind where you sit; that one's Brannock's and he's particular and he's dead, but he was particular.

hub.speaker: Aud Fennick
hub.text: Go on, ask. Everyone wants to and nobody does.

choices.text: Why did you come south?
Your family's bell has stopped ringing.
You're humming a grace with no words in it.
Will you let me walk you to the line?
Is there nothing that would turn you round?
This is the line. I'll stop here.
Hesta wants to know what to do with your bell.
I'll sit a while.

why.speaker: Aud Fennick
why.text: Because I was the last one, dear, and being the last one is a job, and I had done it for eleven years and I had got tired. — That is not sadness. Everybody wants it to be sadness and then they can do something about it. I buried a brother, two sisters and a husband, and I kept the door painted and I went to market and I answered to the name, and one Tollday I was standing at the trestle and I thought: there is nobody this is for. And it was quite a light feeling. I sold the house to Wynstead, gave the linen to Hesta Hollins, and walked.

the_bell.speaker: Aud Fennick
the_bell.text: Has it! — Well, that's neat. It stopped when I stopped answering to the name, I expect; that's how they work, whatever the Wardens say about bronze. — Hesta will be polishing it every dawn and losing sleep over the custom, because she is exactly that sort of woman and it is why I gave her the linen. Tell her from me: take it down, say the name, and go to bed. — Or don't, if you think she'd rather have the seventeen. Or bring it to me and I'll carry it in with me and it can be silent somewhere it matters. — There. Three answers and all of them mine, so none of them are binding. Do as you like. I have given up telling people what to do; it was the other job I was tired of.

the_grace.speaker: Aud Fennick
the_grace.text: The Long Table grace. Merrowby sings it before harvest supper, three hundred people, and it is not a good tune. — I have left the words out. Don't supply them; people try, and then I have to stop. — The words are all names, you see. Whose field, whose oven, whose table, whose year. I can carry the shape of it south. I cannot carry three hundred names into the grey and I will not try and fail at it on the last day. So: the shape, hummed, and everybody who ought to be in it is in it, and nobody has to be named to be there. That is my whole theology and it took me six months in a tent to work out.

the_walk.speaker: Aud Fennick
the_walk.text: Yes. Now, then, before the tents are up and being solemn. — The Order sends someone so that the last thing a body hears is a voice saying something ordinary, and they are quite right, and I have asked for it, and I would like you to know that I asked. Talk about the weather. Talk about the eels. Say something dull and say it the whole way and do not make a speech at the end, and if you cry I shall be very kind about it and I shall also not stop walking.

turning.speaker: Aud Fennick
turning.text: You are a dear for asking and you are the fourth. — No. And I will tell you why not, since you have been decent: because the thing that would turn me round is somebody in Merrowby needing me on a particular Tollday for a particular thing, and there is not one, and there has not been for eleven years, and the whole valley would be very sorry to hear it and not one of them would be able to invent one. That is not cruelty, it is arithmetic. — Now. If you find me one, mind, I am not proud. I would come back for something real. I would not come back for a fuss.

the_fennick_bell_now.speaker: Aud Fennick
the_fennick_bell_now.text: Hesta Hollins has polished a bell that does not ring every morning since the spring and she would like a stranger to tell her to stop. — I shall tell you what I think and then I shall stop telling people what to do, which I gave up on the road and have relapsed into twice. It stopped when I stopped answering to the name. That is not a mystery, dear, it is arithmetic; I did it on purpose on a Tollday at a trestle and the bell agreed with me by Thursday. — So: she takes it down and buries it under the table's foot at the Long Table and sleeps, which is the custom and which is what custom is for. Or it stays up silent because I am alive, which is true and is also a bell in a tree that nobody will ever ring. Or you carry it down here and I take it into the grey with me and it can be silent somewhere it matters.

choices.text: It stays up. You are alive and the village can count to seventeen.
I'll carry it south to you. Take it into the grey.
I'll tell her the Fennicks are gone. Let her bury it and sleep.
I'd rather you told her yourself.

fennick_bell_settled.speaker: Aud Fennick
fennick_bell_settled.text: Then that is settled and neither of us has to have an opinion about it again. — Tell her I said the linen was good linen and that I am cross about the blue cuff, and do not soften it; she will know it is me by the crossness and she will sleep better for it than for anything kind you could invent.

the_line.speaker: Aud Fennick
the_line.text: This is it. You can feel it on the face before you can see it; the grey starts about four paces on and my hands have gone the colour of the road. — You talked about eels for two hours. That was exactly right and I shall not tell you so again. — Here. The bell. The clapper is tied and I tied it myself in Merrowby on the morning I left, so that it could not ring on the way and make a fuss. Take it back to Cadwen; they hang what we leave and ring them all at once on the Ash Winter night, which is very loud and is the only loud thing they do. — Now go back up the road and do not watch. That is not me being brave. It is that you will stand there for an hour if I let you and the light goes early here.

bye.speaker: Aud Fennick
bye.text: Go on. And if you are ever at the Long Table, hum the tune and leave the words out and see who looks up.
